items.summary: We investigate the rigidity of smooth stationary solutions to the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in ℝⁿ with singularities along a linear subspace Σ ≅ ℝᵏ. Assuming the scale-invariant transverse bound ‖u(x)‖ ≤ C‖x′‖⁻¹, where x′ ∈ ℝᵐ represents the transverse coordinates and m = n − k is the codimension of the singularity, we prove that u ≡ 0 provided m ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ k < m. This result generalizes the recent theorem of Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie (2026), which corresponds to the case k = 1 and n ≥ 5. Our proof relies on a quantitative local regularity theorem showing that the transverse bound implies the removability of the singularity along Σ. The argument combines weak extension across the subspace, approximate Green functions for the adjoint drift operator, a one-sided bound for the total head pressure, and a localized Frehse–Růžička weighted estimate followed by a finite Stokes–Morrey bootstrap. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of the codimension threshold m ≥ 4 by constructing non-trivial counterexamples for m = 1, m = 2, and m = 3 via trivial extensions of Jeffery–Hamel and Landau solutions, together with a new explicit family of non-trivial solutions in the borderline case m = 1. Finally, we discuss the technical obstruction preventing the immediate removal of the condition k < m and propose a conditional rigidity result under additional integrability assumptions.
items.title: RIGIDITY OF STATIONARY NAVIER–STOKES SOLUTIONS WITH TRANSVERSE BOUNDS NEAR HIGHER-CODIMENSIONAL SINGULAR SUBSPACES

items.summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
items.title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

items.summary: Version 3 is an organisational change only: the four subsections of the verification section are reordered so that the two Krook levels, the amplitude equation and the Vlasov solver, precede the two with diffusion and drag, the amplitude equation with diffusion and drag and the Vlasov solver with the Fokker–Planck operator. No text, number, figure or table is changed from version 2, and the description below is version 2’s. Version 2 of this paper adds a related-work section placing the work against the analytic quasi-steady theory of Lestz and Duarte (2021), the regime maps of Zhang et al. (2026) and the steady-or-chirping criterion of Duarte et al. (2017, 2018); places the near-marginal comparison against Lestz and Duarte's two validity constraints and withdraws version 1's reading of the 24 percent gap, which is now a candidate explanation and not an established one; relabels the drag ratio of the ITER-like slice as the collisional ratio of Lilley et al. and places the turbulence-corrected ITER ratio, an order of magnitude smaller, between the two steady slices tested; states the comparison with the cold-background regime map at the point where the reduced model fails; narrows three statements of version 1 to what was tested; and adds the experiments version 1 left open, a reverse ramp pair at the first operating point and the edge and a benchmark pair at a second operating point. An erratum corrects a sentence of version 1's Limits section that had the two near-threshold amplitudes reversed: the held level of the full- f solver is 24 percent above the cubic equation's steady state, not the other way round. The paper builds and verifies a two-level reduced model of a fast-ion-driven mode, the Berk–Breizman bump-on-tail problem, as a plant whose purpose is to locate and characterise the regime in which the mode saturates to a steady state, the regime a fusion power plant must stay in. Level 0 is the near-threshold cubic amplitude equation with Krook, diffusive and drag collisions; Level 1 is a full- f one-dimensional Vlasov solver with a Krook operator; Level 2 adds drag and diffusion acting on the departure from the initial distribution. Each level was verified against the literature before its results were used: the amplitude equation reproduces the critical Krook rate 4.4 and the critical diffusion rate 2.05; the Vlasov solver reproduces the linear growth rate and frequency to 0.01 percent, conserves energy to second order, and reproduces the Berk–Breizman saturation law within 4 percent across the steady region and the diffusive saturation formula within 4 to 7 percent away from marginal stability. For the warm distribution used, the external damping on the field is only 87 percent effective as an amplitude damping, so marginal stability lies at a damping of 1.15 times the collisionless drive rather than 1.0; with that correction the full- f solver agrees with the cubic equation on the steady side of the bifurcation near threshold, and saturates 24 percent above it at a finite distance from marginal stability, in the direction and of the size that other simulations have reported against the same theory. The steady region is mapped in the damping–collision plane: with Krook collisions the oscillating region is a tongue at collision rates below 0.3 to 0.4 of the drive, closed above it; with diffusion equal to the drive, with or without drag at 0.7 of diffusion, every damping from 0.1 to 0.9 of the drive is steady, one point still rising at the end of its run; with drag at 1.2 of diffusion no steady point was found, and at the strongest drives the reduced model leaves its validity where a cold-background resonant model saturates steadily. The edge of the steady region along the collision axis lies between diffusion rates of 0.4 and 0.5 of the drive at a damping of 0.5 of the drive, converged on two velocity grids, and within the same bracket at a damping of 0.3, where every steady level is 1.41

items.summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.

The study uses 20,795 images from three public sources, with 20,557 perceptual groups kept intact across experimental partitions. The package covers 212 completed training jobs, including main and component comparisons, classifier-head sensitivity, image-model references, candidate probability banks, and earlier-poisoning experiments. The main comparisons and image-model references use ten deterministic seeds. The classifier-head and GRU-structure study uses three seeds. Included materials comprise dataset manifests and image checksums, perceptual-group metadata, split assignments, seeds and configurations, held-out predictions, candidate probabilities, numerical summaries, result figures, analysis and verification scripts, and scientific execution-source snapshots. Additional fixed-model analyses examine validation availability, validation-label contamination, and artifact retention. The README and reproducibility guide explain verification, reanalysis, environment requirements, and dataset reconstruction. Dataset images and model checkpoints are not included. items.summary: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths is an open-access engineering monograph and interactive instructional module published by the Prep4Uni.Online OER Initiative . This work provides an analytical, undergraduate/postgraduate-level treatment of the computational geometry foundations required to translate three-dimensional surface meshes into layer-by-layer machine toolpaths. Aligned with international accreditation standards—specifically the Washington Accord (WA1–WA5) and EUR-ACE First/Second Cycle frameworks—this publication establishes the mathematical proofs, vector algorithms, and point-in-polygon logic governing modern additive manufacturing slicing software. Core Mathematical & Computational Themes: STL Topology & Facet Representation: Analysis of unstructured triangulated surface meshes, outward unit normal vectors (\(\mathbf{n}\)), vertex coordinate systems, and planar boundary extraction. Parametric Facet-Plane Intersection: Step-by-step vector linear interpolation for deriving the intersection segment \(S_k\) formed by cutting planes at \(z = z_k\), addressing non-manifold edges, vertex touching, and numerical epsilon shifts. Jordan Curve Theorem & Parity Logic: Formal implementation of the 2D Ray-Casting algorithm and Even-Odd Parity test for robust interior, exterior, and internal void classification across arbitrary closed slices. Toolpath Trajectory Generation: Comparative kinematics and geometry between continuous concentric perimeter offset loops and 45° zigzag parallel hatch raster patterns. Formative Assessment Suite: A three-tier verification suite comprising 8 foundational concepts, 7 real-world slicer failure debugging scenarios, and 6 step-by-step quantitative engineering worked examples. Note: The full interactive web edition—featuring client-side HTML5 simulation canvas engines, dynamic parameter sliders, and real-time slice projection mathematics—is accessible at: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/industrial-and-manufacturing-technologies/additive-manufacturing-3d-printing/mathematics-of-slicing/

items.summary: NANOROBOT-ENHANCED DIGITAL TWINS OF BRAIN STATE AT THE LIMIT A multiscale, uncertainty-aware research atlas on microrobotic observations, neural inverse problems, active model discrimination and the limits of computational brain twins. This research monograph asks whether additional microscale observations or strictly bounded reversible experiments can distinguish competing neural-state models that explain conventional measurements equally well. The twin is explicitly defined as a versioned scientific belief, not a digital person, a mind reader or a clinically validated instrument. Its objective is not maximum model complexity but improved identifiability, calibrated prediction under new conditions and faithful retention of failed hypotheses. The work develops five layers: multiscale neural and microenvironment state representation; posterior equivalence and prior sensitivity; non-clinical safe experimental design; frozen-version forking, rollback and reference ancestry; and blind prospective validation against classical state-space systems and independently specified alternatives. Its research architecture includes 30 distinct mathematical derivation plates linked to later chapters, 82 chapters with five independently paginated research sections apiece, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 revisable Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger identifies existing support for brain modeling, latent neural dynamics, experiment design and preclinical microrobot tracking while preventing those sources from being mistaken for evidence of the proposed integrated system. Key research questions include: Can two equally accurate virtual brains be separated by a small, permissible observation? How can the effect of a measurement itself be separated from neural change? When does a prior dominate the inferred brain state? Can the model predict unseen function rather than reconstruct a training signal? Can another laboratory reproduce a rejected twin and safely return to an earlier version? SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This is a forward-looking, non-clinical research synthesis and experimental hypothesis architecture. It provides no personal medical advice, patient-specific interpretations or instruction to deliver neural interventions. Existing murine microrobot tracking and virtual-brain modeling studies do not establish autonomous neural nanorobot readout, human safety, privacy-sensitive mind inference or therapeutic efficacy. Proposed formulas, experiments, research gates and answer embryos are not newly validated biological laws or executed experiments. The work keeps independent safety vetoes, privacy, external reproducibility and explicit model retirement as first-class constraints. Research questions remain open to refutation, correction and reconstruction by future human and AI researchers.

items.summary: This technical note documents a conditional mathematical correspondence between the static spatial kernel used in conventional electromagnetic potential theory and the fixed-source gravitational potential in Lisa Doumbouya’s Harmonic Physics programme. Under supplied three-dimensional Euclidean geometry, spherical symmetry and stated boundary conditions, the derivation gives the static Green function 1/(4πr). Applying the existing gravitational source normalization yields the potential −μ/r, whose radial derivative gives the inward acceleration −μ/r². The note distinguishes potential, field amplitude, intensity, acceleration and optical measurement conversion, keeping geometric normalization separate from the distance exponent. The optical phase-ruler results are reviewed alongside the GRACE-FO forward forecasts. Calibrated reconstruction using measured phase retained micrometre-scale agreement with processed microwave ranging, while some forward models produced much larger errors. These results do not establish exponential error growth or identify a unique physical cause. The correspondence uses established mathematics and remains conditional on the supplied geometry, source calibration and physical interpretation. It does not establish an electromagnetic mechanism of gravity or derive spatial geometry from foundational Phase. The note includes the analytical proof, assumptions, evidence boundaries and requirements for a subsequent physical test. No new experimental data are introduced.

items.summary: Fisher information metric tensors for the 41 held-out SONICOM test subjects, as used in “Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information” (D. Bassett). Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/domfrbassett/fisher-rao-hrtf-upsampling What the tensors are At each of the 793 directions of the SONICOM grid, the 2×2 tensor g = JᵀΣ⁻¹J describes how well the auditory cues separate that direction from its neighbours. J is the spatial Jacobian of the cues: Barumerli monaural PGE features, ILD and MaxIACCe-transformed ITD, each fitted with real spherical harmonics. Σ holds the cue noise (σ_mon = 1.25 dB, σ_ILD = 1 dB, σ_ITD = 0.569). All fields are low-pass filtered at 16 kHz before the cues are extracted. The tensor is expressed in a local tangent basis u₁ = a × r, u₂ = r × u₁, where a = z, or y when |r_z| > 0.9, and its units are d′² per rad². Contents metric_tensors.zip has one folder per subject, metric_tensors/subject_####/ , containing 25 files per subject (1,025 in total): reference_metric_tensor.mat : the dense measured HRTF. <METHOD>_N###_metric_tensor.mat : one file per reconstruction. There are six methods: SUpDEq_SH , SUpDEq_MCA , SUpDEq_NN_MCA_6dB (SUpDEq-Natural-MCA in the paper), SUpDEq_Bary_MCA_6dB , RANF and FSP_AE . Each is reconstructed from N = 100, 19, 5 and 3 retained directions. The 164 natural-neighbour and barycentric files at N = 5 and 3 have status “ not_applicable ”. The interpolation is undefined for those masks, so these files carry no tensors. Variables in each file: metricTensor : the tensors at SH order 6 [2×2×793]. familyGram : per-cue-family Gram matrices JᵀJ before noise weighting, at SH orders 4, 6 and 8 [2×2×793×3 families×3 orders]. They let you recompute the tensors with other noise values or SH orders. In reconstruction files only: crossFamilyGram : the unsymmetrised cross terms J_refᵀ J_recon, same layout as familyGram . airmByDirection : the pointwise AIRM discrepancy from the reference. Metadata: coordinates (Cartesian and azimuth/elevation in degrees), cue band, noise values (reference files only), status (“ completed ” or “ not_applicable ”) and, for not-applicable files, a message giving the reason. SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.

items.summary: This working paper develops a relational Phase interpretation of black holes within the Harmonic Physics research programme, using general relativity, exact Kerr geometry and semiclassical black-hole thermodynamics as its physical baseline. It examines how phase organisation, temporal reference, observer accessibility and information persistence might relate to black-hole closure. Within the proposed framework, a phase-cycle is a closed relational structure that supports recurrence. Measured succession requires distinguishable relations and persistent records, while geometry and causal history are treated as observer-level reconstructions. The temporal-anchor hypothesis concerns a deeper terminal condition at which the parent domain loses the internally usable references needed to resolve further clocks and geometry. This proposed condition is kept distinct from the regular event horizon, across which local evolution continues. Observation is described through a joint observation relation among admitted source organisation, a physical channel and an observer-capable organisation. Source state, coupling and registered record retain separate roles; changes in accessibility may alter registration while the source organisation persists. The paper consolidates three bounded mathematical findings: exact Kerr ingoing and outgoing endpoints can have opposite trapped and anti-trapped orientations with the same mass and spin parameters; spherical source/exterior matching leaves the transition law undetermined; and a leading slow-rotation calculation permits the same sign of angular momentum in closing and opening configurations. These results establish compatibility within the stated geometric constructions. A physical transition mechanism remains to be derived. Black-to-white-hole models provide external theoretical comparisons. Return to the original exterior and the opening of a daughter phase are treated as distinct hypotheses, each requiring an appropriate causal structure, state map and conservation accounting. The remaining requirements include an invariant parent-relative terminal criterion, a physical Phase-to-boundary map, transition dynamics, information and entropy accounting, and a stable nonperturbative rotating completion. The paper remains a developing theoretical interpretation supported by standard-geometry comparisons and bounded symbolic checks. It does not establish a physical black-to-white transition, information recovery through evaporation or a daughter universe. Version 2.3, dated 17 October 2026, updates observation and self-nesting terminology, clarifies geodesic incompleteness and fixed-angular-momentum assumptions, and refreshes the references. The existing displayed equations and reported test results are retained. keywords: Phase Theory; black holes; event horizons; geodesic incompleteness; relational time; phase contraction; information accessibility; singularity; white holes; quantum gravity.

An adaptive algorithm can restore predictive accuracy while obscuring the physical origin of its own correction. This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. The first coupling is the existence of physically traceable internal references that can be challenged against electrically and temporally independent standards. The second is a source-aware drift-diagnostic process that distinguishes electronics gain, electrode-tissue transfer, tissue-like surrogate changes, changing source signals and model/feature drift, explicitly recording instances of nonidentifiability. The third is external functional requalification, which can reject an apparently successful update after hidden-domain testing, material or reference replacement, loss of selectivity, missing raw observations, or inability to reproduce the frozen predecessor. This research monograph is divided into seven causal layers and 82 chapters. Five major subsections of each chapter are assigned independent pages, yielding 410 separately paginated technical essays. Thirty gold mathematical derivations are linked from chapter-opening equations to discriminating experiments. The mathematics includes augmented state-space observability, nonlinear observation functions, source-separation Jacobians, Kalman innovations, impedance spectroscopy, covariance propagation, change-point statistics, conformal coverage, selective risk, hard-veto constrained update eligibility, reference-bridge covariance, exact rollback and cross-laboratory requalification. A displayed formula is a candidate analytical instrument with stated dimensions and assumptions, not a discovered biological law. Two hundred detailed Research Gates are preserved at the rear: 82 interrogate source identifiability, another 82 challenge independent physical and evidential hard vetoes, and 36 require third-party reconstruction of a frozen reference history. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose revisable architectures, beginning with the Neural Interface Calibration Passport. The Passport ties an interface's physical identity to the raw analog and digitized record, calibrated unit chain, hardware reference ancestors, model and feature checksums, reasons for changing any reference, failed updates, revoked permissions, blinded requalification and rollback. These are proposed evidence structures, not commercially validated devices. The DOI bibliography contains 18 unique external research records covering chronic intracortical signal instability, low-dimensional BCI stabilization, decoder adaptation, long-term electrode-tissue behavior, complex impedance metrology, electrochemical reference limits, neural interface materials and conformal uncertainty under covariate shift. items.summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.

items.summary: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths is an open-access engineering monograph and interactive instructional module published by the Prep4Uni.Online OER Initiative . This work provides an analytical, undergraduate/postgraduate-level treatment of the computational geometry foundations required to translate three-dimensional surface meshes into layer-by-layer machine toolpaths. Aligned with international accreditation standards—specifically the Washington Accord (WA1–WA5) and EUR-ACE First/Second Cycle frameworks—this publication establishes the mathematical proofs, vector algorithms, and point-in-polygon logic governing modern additive manufacturing slicing software. items.summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
items.title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

items.summary: We investigate the rigidity of smooth stationary solutions to the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in ℝⁿ with singularities along a linear subspace Σ ≅ ℝᵏ. Assuming the scale-invariant transverse bound ‖u(x)‖ ≤ C‖x′‖⁻¹, where x′ ∈ ℝᵐ represents the transverse coordinates and m = n − k is the codimension of the singularity, we prove that u ≡ 0 provided m ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ k < m. This result generalizes the recent theorem of Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie (2026), which corresponds to the case k = 1 and n ≥ 5. Our proof relies on a quantitative local regularity theorem showing that the transverse bound implies the removability of the singularity along Σ. The argument combines weak extension across the subspace, approximate Green functions for the adjoint drift operator, a one-sided bound for the total head pressure, and a localized Frehse–Růžička weighted estimate followed by a finite Stokes–Morrey bootstrap. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of the codimension threshold m ≥ 4 by constructing non-trivial counterexamples for m = 1, m = 2, and m = 3 via trivial extensions of Jeffery–Hamel and Landau solutions, together with a new explicit family of non-trivial solutions in the borderline case m = 1. Finally, we discuss the technical obstruction preventing the immediate removal of the condition k < m and propose a conditional rigidity result under additional integrability assumptions.

items.summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
items.title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

items.summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.
items.title: PRB-WM: Physics-Regularized Beta World Models for Predictive Link Adaptation on Real Time-Varying Underwater Acoustic Channels

items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
items.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition

items.summary: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.
items.title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control

items.summary: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. We prove that inter-agent collision avoidance is guaranteed provided communication staleness remains bounded. As the reachable set inflates between state transmissions, each agent reasons about when to preemptively transmit its state information to neighboring agents based on novel metrics characterizing uncertainty risk and kinematic risk. We implement and simulate a variety of pursuit-evasion scenarios and show that preemptive communication reduces messages by 77.5% compared to periodic and event-triggered baselines with zero collisions.
items.title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions
